Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment ( n = 166), M segment ( n = 48), and S segment ( n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L ( R 2 = 0.069), M ( R 2 = 0.021), and S ( R 2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.

source_records.abstract: Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment ( n = 166), M segment ( n = 48), and S segment ( n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L ( R 2 = 0.069), M ( R 2 = 0.021), and S ( R 2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.

papers.title: Predictive Surveillance for Andes Virus Transmission in the Americas.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations in conventional, case-based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person-to-person transmission. In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.
papers.journal: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene

analysis_zh.methods: 本文为观点与分析文章;未报告任何原始数据收集、研究设计或样本细节。(A2)
analysis_zh.results: 选定的预测模型整合流行病学、气候、环境和啮齿类相关变量,可能提供2至12个月的预警窗口,具体取决于情境和数据输入。(A3)
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者认为,AI支持的生态一体化预测监测可通过指导风险沟通、啮齿类监测、实验室准备和针对性公共卫生行动,补充传统监测。(A6)
analysis_zh.limitations: 该工作为概念性研究,缺乏原始实证数据;结论依赖现有证据,摘要提供的方法细节有限。(A5)

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. papers.title: The 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a renewed call for global zoonotic preparedness
papers.abstract: The 2026 cluster of Andes virus (ANDV) infection linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius resulted in 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable), including three deaths, and required the monitoring of more than 650 contacts across more than 30 countries and territories before the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026. Available evidence suggests a single land-based zoonotic exposure before embarkation, followed by limited person-to-person transmission on board. Although WHO assessed the global risk as low throughout, the event exposed recurring weaknesses in zoonotic preparedness, including delayed clinical recognition in a remote setting, maritime outbreak protocols oriented toward other pathogens, and the burden of multinational contact tracing for an infection with an incubation period of up to 6 weeks. This editorial examines these lessons in light of earlier ANDV outbreaks and argues for closer integration of One Health surveillance, maritime health security, and the International Health Regulations in preparing for rare but high-consequence zoonoses.
papers.journal: International Journal of Surgery: Global Health

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next- generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management. KEYWORDS acute pancreatitis, case report, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, Seoul orthohantavirus Introduction Case presentation and clinical data A 33-year-old man presented with one week of recurrent fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He had no history of gallstones, hypertriglyceridemia, alcohol abuse, or other recognized risk factors for acute pancreatitis. Although viral gastroenteritis could explain fever, vomiting and watery diarrhea, the presence of epigastric tenderness on TYPE Case Report PUBLISHED 28 October 2026 DOI 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 01 frontiersin.org physical examination together with marked peripancreatic- perirenal exudates identified on initial abdominal CT raised strong clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. Initial non-contrast abdominal CT showed peripancreatic and perirenal haziness, renal fascial thickening, and small-volume abdominopelvic effusion with mild pancreatic swelling, findings highly suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis (Figure 1). Initial supportive measures for suspected acute pancreatitis were implemented, including intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, octreotide infusion, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, and volume resuscitation. Of note, severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 109/L) was already documented on admission rather than developing during hospitalization. However, the patient demonstrated progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without biochemical elevation of pancreatic enzymes. Two abdominal CT examinations were performed: a non- contrast CT on hospital day 1 (admission), followed by contrast- enhanced abdominal CT on hospital day 2. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed progressive retroperitoneal exudation accompanied by newly developed bilateral pleural effusion and splenomegaly. Routine work-up for undifferentiated fever was sent before mNGS testing, including bacterial blood cultures, stool culture, and a respiratory-borne viral screening panel, all of which returned negative results. Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) laboratory screening was not performed because clinical suspicion for TMA was low: the patient lacked schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, had no severe neurologic manifestations, and mNGS rapidly identified Seoul orthohantavirus as the causative pathogen. Whole-blood mNGS detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus (HBV) and no bacterial or fungal pathogens. Hepatoprotective therapy consisted of intravenous reduced glutathione and magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate. Due to persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and unstable clinical status precluding oral feeding, the patient was kept nil per os (NPO) at admission, not as a standard mandatory intervention for suspected acute pancreatitis. Enteral nutrition was gradually initiated once abdominal symptoms improved. After supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, albumin supplementation, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction, the patient recovered fully; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology (Figure 2). Laboratory and imaging findings Initial laboratory investigations showed a mixed acid-base disturbance, characterized by respiratory alkalosis with normal anion-gap (AnGap 2-10 mmol/L),hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and liver function injury. The most striking abnormality was profound thrombocytopenia (29 × 109/L); urinalysis revealed hematuria and proteinuria. Table 2 was revised to add serum amylase, lipase, serum triglyceride, serum urea, serum creatinine, sodium, potassium, hemoglobin values. Reticulocyte count was not tested in clinical practice; hemoglobin levels over serial time-points are presented to evaluate for bone-marrow suppression. Urine sediment examination did not demonstrate granular or hyaline casts. Serial urine output was prospectively recorded as part of intensive care monitoring; overall urine output remained adequate throughout hospitalization without anuria or oliguric renal failure. Mild anemia was observed (minimum hemoglobin 127 g/L). Serial changes in leukocytes, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, transaminases, platelets, albumin, and coagulation parameters are summarized in Table 2. The dynamic clinical, laboratory, imaging, and management course across hospitalization is summarized in the diagnostic timeline (Table 1). Hospital course and management The initial working diagnosis was suspected severe acute pancreatitis, and management comprised nil-per-os status due to patient intolerance of oral intake, octreotide infusion, a proton- pump inhibitor, empirical antimicrobial therapy, and fluid resuscitation. When the severe thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction could not be explained by primary pancreatitis, HFRS was considered. On hospital day 3, whole-blood mNGS returned high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, confirming the diagnosis. Treatment was adjusted to include intravenous immunoglobulin, human albumin, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction. Abdominal pain resolved, and platelet count, liver, and renal parameters gradually normalized. The patient was discharged on hospital day 11 in good clinical condition, with outpatient follow-up scheduled for monitoring of liver function and HBV. Discussion This case highlights a diagnostically challenging presentation in which Seoul orthohantavirus infection clinically and radiologically mimicked severe acute pancreatitis, underscoring the need to consider HFRS in the differential diagnosis of unexplained pancreatitis-like presentations (1). Acute pancreatitis is a recognized but rare complication of HFRS (2, 6), and its distinction from hantavirus-induced pancreatic involvement is notoriously difficult because of overlapping clinical and imaging features (9). The present case further illustrates that peripancreatic exudation and retroperitoneal fluid —hallmark findings of severe acute pancreatitis—can also result from the profound systemic capillary leakage and retroperitoneal edema characteristic of hantavirus infection (4, 5). In this context, marked thrombocytopenia, renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, and the absence of typical pancreatitis risk factors constituted pivotal clues that prompted consideration of an alternative etiology (9). Moreover, the normal pancreatic enzyme levels observed here demonstrate that Abbreviations HFRS, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; AP, acute pancreatitis; SAP, severe acute pancreatitis; CT, computed tomography; mNGS, metagenomic next-generation sequencing; HBV, hepatitis B virus; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; IVIG, intravenous immunoglobulin; PLT, platelet count; DIC, disseminated intravascular coagulation. Liu and Song 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 02 frontiersin.org biochemical markers alone cannot reliably exclude HFRS in suspected pancreatitis (10). It should be acknowledged that severe acute pancreatitis itself may produce thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction secondary to systemic inflammation. However, several features argued against primary acute pancreatitis in this patient: thrombocytopenia was already present at initial presentation as a critical-value finding before any expected inflammatory peak of pancreatitis; renal injury was accompanied by prominent urinary findings (hematuria and proteinuria) typical for hantavirus-mediated tubular injury rather than purely pre-renal renal impairment secondary to pancreatitis-related hypovolemia; and serum amylase/lipase remained within normal reference ranges throughout admission despite extensive peripancreatic exudates on CT imaging. The dynamic imaging feature observed in this case— progressive retroperitoneal exudation on contrast-enhanced CT accompanied by relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes —merits particular attention in the differential diagnosis of hantavirus infection presenting with abdominal manifestations. While AP is a recognized complication of HFRS, the typical CT findings in such cases commonly include pancreatic FIGURE 1 Serial axial abdominal computed tomography (CT) images of Seoul orthohantavirus-associated capillary-leak syndrome mimicking severe acute pancreatitis. (A, C) Non-contrast abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 1 (admission). White arrows indicate the pancreas, peripancreatic fat- stranding inflammatory exudates, and thickened bilateral prerenal fascia with perirenal exudates. These radiological features initially raised high clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. (B, D) Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 2. Compared with hospital day 1 non-contrast CT, retroperitoneal, peripancreatic and perirenal exudates are obviously progressive. After contrast administration, the pancreatic parenchyma shows no definite necrosis or large-scale parenchymal destruction. FIGURE 2 Pre-discharge abdominal ultrasound obtained on hospital day 12 (at discharge). (A) Color-Doppler ultrasound view of upper abdomen. (B) Grayscale two-dimensional ultrasound image. White arrows mark the pancreatic gland. The pancreas presents normal parenchymal echotexture, without swelling, enlargement or surrounding fluid-collection, confirming complete resolution of previous retro-peritoneal inflammatory exudative lesions. Liu and Song 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 03 frontiersin.org enlargement, peripancreatic edema, and occasionally necrosis or hemorrhage (4). However, extensive retroperitoneal involvement with a relatively preserved pancreatic gland reflects the underlying pathophysiological hallmark of hantavirus infection —virus-induced increased microvascular permeability leading to fluid extravasation into the retroperitoneal space. Indeed, the retroperitoneum has been identified as a major site of vascular leak in HFRS (11), and established evidence indicates that hantavirus elicits a robust inflammatory cascade with cytokine release and endothelial dysfunction that can produce extensive retroperitoneal fluid accumulation even in the absence of true pancreatic necrosis (12, 13). Prior case reports of HFRS mimicking acute pancreatitis have generally relied on single- time-point scans and could not capture this evolving radiological signature (7). Recognition of this distinctive pattern is of substantial practical importance, particularly in endemic regions (14, 15). From a clinical standpoint, progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic changes on follow-up CT, when accompanied by thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction, should prompt clinicians to broaden the differential beyond pancreatic pathology. Attributing the initial retroperitoneal exudation and abdominopelvic effusion to severe acute pancreatitis follows a conventional diagnostic pathway, given that such radiological findings are well-recognized features of this condition. However, the subsequent constellation of profound thrombocytopenia, progressive renal impairment, and urinary abnormalities extended beyond the typical scope of pancreatic pathology and prompted re-evaluation of the initial diagnostic assumption (9). This scenario illustrates a classic diagnostic pitfall, where an initially plausible diagnosis supported by compelling imaging can lead to anchoring bias that delays consideration of alternative etiologies with similar radiological features. Indeed, various infections mimic the clinical and radiological presentation of acute pancreatitis, including viral pathogens that also cause systemic thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction (16, 17); beyond pancreatitis, hantavirus infection can mimic other acute abdominal emergencies such as acute appendicitis (18, 19). analysis.background: HFRS is a zoonotic orthohantavirus disease marked by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak; its atypical forms can closely resemble acute pancreatitis, creating diagnostic difficulty.
analysis.methods: A single 33‑year‑old man was evaluated; initial non‑contrast CT showed peripancreatic and perirenal exudates, followed by contrast‑enhanced CT demonstrating progressive retroperitoneal exudation and mild pancreatic changes; whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed for pathogen identification.
analysis.results: The patient had profound thrombocytopenia (platelet nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, and no elevation of pancreatic enzymes; imaging revealed extensive retroperitoneal fluid with relatively preserved pancreas and new pleural effusion; mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (and hepatitis B virus); after supportive care, immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment, he recovered fully and post‑discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology.
analysis.contribution: The report highlights that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically, identifies key diagnostic clues (disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, preserved pancreas), and demonstrates that mNGS enables rapid definitive pathogen confirmation to guide appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based on a single case report, limiting generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS, caused by orthohantaviruses, can mimic acute pancreatitis, complicating diagnosis. Methods: A 33‑year‑old man underwent CT imaging and whole‑blood mNGS to identify the pathogen. Results: He presented with severe thrombocytopenia (29 × 10⁹/L), renal dysfunction, and retroperitoneal exudation; mNGS detected high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered with supportive care and normal pancreas on follow‑up ultrasound. Contribution: The case shows Seoul orthohantavirus can closely resemble severe pancreatitis, underscores diagnostic clues, and illustrates mNGS utility for early pathogen confirmation. Limitations: Single‑patient case report limits broader applicability.

papers.title: Integrated in Silico Method for Virtual Screening and Interaction Profiling of Repurposed and Natural Inhibitor Candidates Against the Rdrp of the Newly Reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 Orthohantavirus
papers.abstract: Introduction: The rapid release of complete viral genome sequences enables early computational prioritization of antiviral candidates before experimental screening becomes available. Objectives: This study evaluated the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp; L protein) of the newly reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 orthohantavirus as an antiviral drug-design target. Methods: The L-segment-derived RdRp sequence was obtained from the public Virological.org report, modeled with AlphaFold, inspected against the NCBI Conserved Domain Database, and submitted to CB-Dock2 for binding-cavity prediction. The predicted pocket (X = 5.872, Y = 29.895, Z = -5.566) was used for DrugRep screening of 100 FDA-approved/repurposed and 100 natural TCMML compounds, which were then independently rescored with KDeep. Results: In the repurposed library, DB00511 and DB11581 gave the strongest DrugRep scores (-10.2), whereas DB00864 gave the highest KDeep pIC50 (7.1249); consensus ranking prioritized DB00511, DB00390 and DB01396. In the natural-product library, T0295 scored best with DrugRep (-9.8) and T8166 with KDeep (7.3537); consensus ranking prioritized T8166, T0295, T6473 and T3809. Interaction analysis supported these candidates through recurrent hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic contacts, including GLU129, SER157, THR170, ALA1463, TRP1464, ARG1544 and GLU1545. Conclusions: The combined DrugRep-KDeep-interaction workflow provides a rational computational shortlist for downstream redocking, molecular dynamics, ADMET profiling and experimental prioritization.

papers.title: A Case Report of Hantavirus Capillary Leak Syndrome in the Southwestern United States.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. We report the case of a previously healthy 20-year-old man who initially presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive weakness after occupational exposure on a ranch in southwestern Arizona. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. In endemic areas with rodent exposure history, hemoconcentration and thrombocytopenia, along with signs of volume overload and rapidly progressive acute respiratory failure, should raise suspicion for hantavirus infection. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control.
