papers.full_text: A Case Report of Hantavirus Capillary Leak Syndrome in the Southwestern United States Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. We report the case of a previously healthy 20‐year‐old man who initially presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive weakness after occupational exposure on a ranch in southwestern Arizona. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. In endemic areas with rodent exposure history, hemoconcentration and thrombocytopenia, along with signs of volume overload and rapidly progressive acute respiratory failure, should raise suspicion for hantavirus infection. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped single‐stranded RNA viruses that can cause zoonotic diseases in humans, including the two most common, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). HFRS is caused by Old World orthohantaviruses and is seen in Asia and Europe. Whereas, HCPS was first identified in the southwestern United States in the early 1990s and is caused by New World hantaviruses. The primary route of transmission is inhalation of aerosolized particles from the urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents. Although HCPS is rare with an annual incidence of 0.04 to 0.19 cases/million persons, it is associated with a high mortality rate ranging from 30% to 50% and poses a diagnostic challenge due to its nonspecific prodromal symptoms. The disease typically progresses from a febrile phase to a rapidly deteriorating cardiopulmonary phase characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypotension, and shock resulting from widespread capillary leak. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a combination of epidemiological context, laboratory abnormalities such as thrombocytopenia and elevated hematocrit, and a high index of suspicion, particularly in endemic regions. We present a case of severe HCPS in a previously healthy young man who developed profound capillary leak syndrome with respiratory failure and shock. This case emphasizes the diagnostic importance of gastrointestinal‐predominant prodromal symptoms, early risk stratification, and timely escalation of supportive care. Per institutional policy, this single‐patient case report did not require formal Institutional Review Board approval. No written consent has been obtained from the patients as there is no patient identifiable data included in this case report. 2. Case Presentation A 20‐year‐old man with no known medical history presented to an outside hospital with over six days of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and generalized weakness. He had recently returned from a vacation in Mexico, where he was evaluated at an urgent care center for similar symptoms and was treated symptomatically with intravenous fluids and antiemetics. Upon his return to southwestern Arizona, where he worked on a ranch, he sought further evaluation in the emergency department due to persistent symptoms. He was febrile but hemodynamically stable on presentation. Laboratory results were notable for leukocytosis with neutrophilia (white cell count 38,100 cells/μL), bandemia (10.4%), hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 20.3 g/dL, hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), lactic acidosis (4.8 mmol/L), and elevated procalcitonin (2.43 ng/mL). Chest CT (Figure 1A) revealed patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities, which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Subsequently, he became progressively hypoxic and hypotensive, requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Patient samples were pan‐cultured, and broad‐spectrum antibiotics were started. Chest CT on presentation (A) showing patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions; and three days later (B) showing worsening pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions suggestive of capillary leak, leading to the placement of bilateral chest tubes. The patient was subsequently transferred to our center for a higher level of care and evaluation for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). He was maintained on lung‐protective ventilation (tidal volume 5.6 mL/kg, PEEP 12, and FiO2 70%–100%). Empiric antibiotics (piperacillin‐tazobactam, vancomycin, and doxycycline), stress‐dose steroids, and vasopressor support (norepinephrine 11 mcg/min, vasopressin 0.03 U/min) were continued. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left and right heart function with a small pericardial effusion. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures showed no microbial growth. Respiratory viral panels, bacterial cultures, and fungal serologies were negative. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for hematologic malignancies. On Day 3, a repeat chest CT showed worsening pulmonary edema, patchy peribronchovascular ground‐glass opacities that may represent alveolar edema, interlobular septal thickening, and large bilateral pleural effusions with adjacent atelectasis (Figure 1B); diuretics were started to maintain a net negative fluid balance (at least–1L every day). Bilateral chest tubes were placed, draining 1L of serous fluid each, and pleural fluid studies revealed a cell count of 129 (45% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 30% macrophages), a pleural fluid protein level of 2.5 g/dL (serum protein 5.3 g/dL), and a pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 301 U/L (serum LDH 648 U/L, upper limit of normal 243 U/L). His B‐type natriuretic peptide was elevated (527.8 pg/mL). Abdominal CT also showed signs of volume overload with small‐volume ascites, pelvic free fluid, mesenteric edema, and diffuse anasarca; diuresis continued. He was gradually weaned off vasopressors, and ventilator parameters including FiO2 and PEEP gradually decreased. He was successfully extubated to a high‐flow nasal cannula on Day 5, and antibiotics were discontinued. His clinical status and laboratory abnormalities gradually improved (Figures 2 and 3), and his right and left chest tubes were removed on Days 8 and 9, respectively. The patient was net negative at 10.9 L during his inpatient stay. Additionally, antinuclear, antiglomerular basement membrane, myeloperoxidase, and serine protease‐3 antibodies were negative. He was discharged home 10 days after presentation with outpatient follow‐up. Eventually, ELISA testing for hantavirus IgM and IgG returned positive from a reference laboratory about 10 days after presentation, confirming the diagnosis of HCPS. Chest CT two days after bilateral chest tube insertion and diuresis showed improvement with scattered ground‐glass opacities and decreased small bilateral pleural effusions. Trends in laboratory results during the patient’s hospital stay reflect the transition from cardiopulmonary phase to convalescence. The patient was extubated and vasopressors were stopped on day 5. Right and left chest tubes were removed on day 8 and 9, respectively. 3. Discussion Since the initial recognition of HCPS during the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, approximately 30 cases have been reported annually in the United States. HCPS most commonly affects previously healthy young adults with occupational or environmental rodent exposure. Over 20 strains of hantaviruses can cause HCPS, but the primary culprits are Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus in North and South America, respectively. Rodents excrete hantaviruses in saliva, urine, and feces, and humans are infected when inhaling the secreted viruses or rarely by rodent bites. This case illustrates a classical but diagnostically challenging presentation of HCPS in a young ranch worker with substantial exposure to rodent‐contaminated environments. 3.1. Gastrointestinal‐Predominant Prodrome as a Diagnostic Pitfall The incubation period of hantavirus ranges from 1 to 3 weeks. The prodromal phase of HCPS frequently resembles a nonspecific viral or gastrointestinal illness and may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea before overt respiratory symptoms develop. Gastrointestinal‐predominant presentations may delay diagnosis because clinicians often initially prioritize gastroenteritis, abdominal sepsis, arboviral disease, or other infectious syndromes. In this case, several bedside “red flags” increased suspicion for HCPS despite the nonspecific prodrome: severe thrombocytopenia, marked hemoconcentration, granulocytic left shift, rapid respiratory deterioration, and rodent exposure in an endemic region. Clinicians at the University of New Mexico developed five criteria to guide clinical decisions and make a presumptive diagnosis during this phase: thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, granulocytic left shift, absence of toxic changes, and more than 10% immunoblasts. Blood smears meeting four of five criteria had high sensitivity (96%), specificity (99%), and positive predictive value (83%) for infection. Notably, our patient met the criteria, and confirmatory testing for hantavirus was dispatched at this stage. 3.2. Differential Diagnosis and Early Clinical Decision‐Making This case highlights two critical clinical decision‐making windows. During the initial prodromal phase, differential considerations included viral gastroenteritis, leptospirosis, dengue/arboviral infections, bacterial sepsis, rickettsioses, influenza‐like illness, Epstein–Barr virus, human bocavirus, hematologic malignancies, and abdominal sources of infection. As the patient progressed to respiratory failure and shock, the differential expanded to include severe sepsis‐associated ARDS, vasculitis with diffuse alveolar injury or pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Goodpasture syndrome), Aspergillus, Pneumocystis, Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Q fever, and HCPS. Several features substantially increased the likelihood of HCPS: rapid onset pulmonary edema with preserved cardiac function, thrombocytopenia, marked hemoconcentration, diffuse capillary leak, and epidemiologic exposure to rodent‐contaminated ranch environments. The broad diagnostic evaluation was appropriate because early HCPS frequently mimics other severe infectious and inflammatory syndromes. 3.3. Pathophysiology of Capillary Leak and Pulmonary Edema Pathogenesis of hantavirus infection is characterized by increased vascular permeability, as the virus principally targets endothelial cells of pulmonary and renal capillaries. It is hypothesized that alpha and beta‐3 integrins act as hantavirus receptors on endothelial cells, and their inactivation contributes to the deregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, leading to altered expression and internalization of vascular endothelial cadherins, damaging the endothelial barrier. In HCPS, this accounts for the capillary leak syndrome by pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, hemoconcentration, hypotension, ascites, mesenteric edema, and anasarca, all of which were present in this patient. Thrombocytopenia is a common and early marker of disease severity and is thought to result from increased endothelial activation and consumption. Although echocardiography demonstrated preserved ventricular systolic function, BNP elevation raised consideration of transient myocardial involvement, which has been described in HCPS. Therefore, pulmonary edema in HCPS may reflect a mixed process involving both severe endothelial leak and variable myocardial depression. In this case, preserved ventricular function and the overall hemodynamic pattern favored predominantly noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. 3.4. Risk Stratification and Escalation of Care This patient presented with several features associated with severe HCPS, including profound thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, vasopressor‐dependent shock, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, diffuse pulmonary edema, and elevated lactate levels. These high‐risk features justified early transfer to an ECMO center and close hemodynamic monitoring. Despite his severe presentation, the patient experienced favorable recovery without ECMO support. Potential explanations include early recognition of capillary leak physiology, prompt intensive care support, lung‐protective ventilation, vasopressor therapy, conservative fluid management, patient age, gender, and the absence of significant medical comorbidities. Recent systematic review data emphasize the importance of early referral to an ECMO center for advanced supportive therapies in severe HCPS. 3.5. Current and Emerging Therapies Management of HCPS remains largely supportive. Mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic support, conservative fluid management, and early recognition of capillary leak physiology are central to care. Venoarterial ECMO may be used in cases with cardiac index < 2.5 L/minute/m2 despite pressor and inotropic support. Small placebo‐controlled studies using ribavirin or high‐dose methylprednisolone did not show clear benefits. A nonrandomized pre‐ and postintervention study (ISRCTN72088243) to assess the efficacy of tocilizumab in reducing mortality in HCPS is underway in Argentina. A recent case‐series based on this trial seemed to show some promise for IL‐6 inhibition in four of the five HCPS patients who survived to ICU discharge after treatment with tocilizumab. However, given the high mortality and a lack of established treatment options, prevention of hantavirus infection by implementing measures to limit contact with rodents is of utmost importance. 3.6. Epidemiology and Long‐Term Outcomes Arizona and the broader Four Corners region remain endemic areas for Sin Nombre virus transmission because of persistent deer mouse reservoirs and environmental exposure risks in rural settings. Occupational exposure involving barns, feed storage areas, sweeping of rodent‐contaminated spaces, and aerosolization of rodent excreta remain important risk factors for infection. Long‐term outcomes among HCPS survivors remain incompletely characterized. Although many patients recover functional independence, persistent fatigue, exertional intolerance, and psychological distress have been reported after severe disease. In this case, the patient demonstrated favorable short‐term recovery and was able to return to routine activities within weeks of discharge, although mild exertional fatigue persisted at follow‐up. 4. Conclusion The strength of this case report lies in serologic confirmation of Hantavirus using ELISA and elaborate clinical details on its presentation, complications, and management. Although it is limited to a single patient, it underscores the diagnostic complexity and clinical severity of HCPS. Notably, gastrointestinal‐predominant prodromal symptoms may obscure early recognition and delay diagnosis. Although rare, HCPS should remain high on the differential for patients presenting with hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, rapid‐onset respiratory failure, and shock, especially in endemic regions with known rodent exposure. Early risk stratification, aggressive supportive management, and timely referral to centers capable of advanced cardiopulmonary support are essential to optimize outcomes. We present a case of severe HCPS in a previously healthy young man who developed profound capillary leak syndrome with respiratory failure and shock. This case emphasizes the diagnostic importance of gastrointestinal‐predominant prodromal symptoms, early risk stratification, and timely escalation of supportive care. Per institutional policy, this single‐patient case report did not require formal Institutional Review Board approval. No written consent has been obtained from the patients as there is no patient identifiable data included in this case report. 2. Case Presentation A 20‐year‐old man with no known medical history presented to an outside hospital with over six days of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and generalized weakness. He had recently returned from a vacation in Mexico, where he was evaluated at an urgent care center for similar symptoms and was treated symptomatically with intravenous fluids and antiemetics. Upon his return to southwestern Arizona, where he worked on a ranch, he sought further evaluation in the emergency department due to persistent symptoms. He was febrile but hemodynamically stable on presentation. Laboratory results were notable for leukocytosis with neutrophilia (white cell count 38,100 cells/μL), bandemia (10.4%), hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 20.3 g/dL, hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), lactic acidosis (4.8 mmol/L), and elevated procalcitonin (2.43 ng/mL). Chest CT (Figure 1A) revealed patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities, which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Subsequently, he became progressively hypoxic and hypotensive, requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Patient samples were pan‐cultured, and broad‐spectrum antibiotics were started. Chest CT on presentation (A) showing patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions; and three days later (B) showing worsening pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions suggestive of capillary leak, leading to the placement of bilateral chest tubes. The patient was subsequently transferred to our center for a higher level of care and evaluation for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). He was maintained on lung‐protective ventilation (tidal volume 5.6 mL/kg, PEEP 12, and FiO2 70%–100%). Empiric antibiotics (piperacillin‐tazobactam, vancomycin, and doxycycline), stress‐dose steroids, and vasopressor support (norepinephrine 11 mcg/min, vasopressin 0.03 U/min) were continued. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left and right heart function with a small pericardial effusion. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures showed no microbial growth. Respiratory viral panels, bacterial cultures, and fungal serologies were negative. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for hematologic malignancies. On Day 3, a repeat chest CT showed worsening pulmonary edema, patchy peribronchovascular ground‐glass opacities that may represent alveolar edema, interlobular septal thickening, and large bilateral pleural effusions with adjacent atelectasis (Figure 1B); diuretics were started to maintain a net negative fluid balance (at least–1L every day). Bilateral chest tubes were placed, draining 1L of serous fluid each, and pleural fluid studies revealed a cell count of 129 (45% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 30% macrophages), a pleural fluid protein level of 2.5 g/dL (serum protein 5.3 g/dL), and a pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 301 U/L (serum LDH 648 U/L, upper limit of normal 243 U/L). His B‐type natriuretic peptide was elevated (527.8 pg/mL). Abdominal CT also showed signs of volume overload with small‐volume ascites, pelvic free fluid, mesenteric edema, and diffuse anasarca; diuresis continued. He was gradually weaned off vasopressors, and ventilator parameters including FiO2 and PEEP gradually decreased. He was successfully extubated to a high‐flow nasal cannula on Day 5, and antibiotics were discontinued. His clinical status and laboratory abnormalities gradually improved (Figures 2 and 3), and his right and left chest tubes were removed on Days 8 and 9, respectively. The patient was net negative at 10.9 L during his inpatient stay. Additionally, antinuclear, antiglomerular basement membrane, myeloperoxidase, and serine protease‐3 antibodies were negative. He was discharged home 10 days after presentation with outpatient follow‐up. analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors present a single‑patient case report of a previously healthy 20‑year‑old man from southwestern Arizona who presented with gastrointestinal symptoms after occupational rodent exposure (A3); laboratory testing showed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%) and thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/µL) (A4); his clinical course required intubation, vasopressor support, and chest CT imaging demonstrating pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions (A6, A7); diagnosis was confirmed by serum ELISA positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG (A9).
analysis.results: The patient rapidly progressed to septic shock, non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (A4, A6); despite aggressive diuresis and bilateral chest tubes, he improved with supportive care and was discharged after extubation and rehabilitation (A8, A9).
analysis.contribution: The report underscores the diagnostic challenge of HCPS when gastrointestinal prodromes dominate, emphasizes the need for early suspicion based on hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and rapid respiratory decline (A10, A11), and reinforces that identification and supportive care are the mainstays of treatment, with ECMO considered in severe cases (A12, A13).
analysis.limitations: As a single‑patient case report, the findings lack generalizability and no formal Institutional Review Board approval or patient consent was required (F23, F24).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS is a rare, often fatal disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted via aerosolized rodent excreta. Methods: A 20‑year‑old man from southwestern Arizona with GI symptoms after rodent exposure was evaluated; labs showed hematocrit 58% and platelets 17,000/µL, imaging revealed pulmonary edema, and ELISA confirmed hantavirus infection. Results: He progressed to septic shock and respiratory failure requiring ventilation, but improved with supportive care and was discharged. Contribution: The case highlights diagnostic difficulty when GI symptoms predominate, the importance of early suspicion using lab and exposure clues, and that supportive care is essential, with ECMO as a possible adjunct. Limitations: Single‑case report with limited generalizability and no IRB or consent required.

papers.title_zh: 关于美国西南部汉坦病毒毛细血管漏综合征的病例报告。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)是一种罕见但致死率高的病毒性疾病,流行于美洲,主要通过吸入被气溶胶化的啮齿动物排泄物传播(A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者报告了一例单患者病例,患者为一名来自亚利桑那州西南部、既往健康的20岁男性,因职业性啮齿动物暴露后出现胃肠道症状(A3);实验室检测显示血液浓缩(血细胞比容58%)和血小板减少(17,000个/μL)(A4);其临床过程需要气管插管、血管加压药支持,并进行胸部CT显示肺水肿和双侧胸腔积液(A6、A7);诊断通过血清ELISA检测汉坦病毒 IgM和IgG阳性得到确认(A9)。
analysis_zh.results: 患者迅速进展为脓毒性休克、非心源性肺水肿和需机械通气的呼吸衰竭(A4、A6);尽管进行了积极的利尿和双侧胸腔引流,他在支持治疗下病情好转,并在拔管及康复后出院(A8、A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该报告强调了在胃肠前驱症状占主导时HCPS的诊断挑战,强调需依据血液浓缩、血小板减少和快速呼吸功能恶化进行早期怀疑(A10、A11),并重申病原体鉴定和支持治疗是治疗的基石,严重病例可考虑使用ECMO(A12、A13)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 作为单患者病例报告,研究结果缺乏普遍适用性,且无需正式的机构审查委员会批准或患者同意(F23、F24)。

papers.title: Hantavirus on a Cruise Ship: What COVID-19 Taught Us.
papers.abstract: Delayed recognition of the mechanics of aerosol transmission-the primary mode of spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-at the beginning of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic led to inadequate early recommendations regarding nonpharmaceutical interventions and poor initial messaging about how to reduce infection risk. We highlight key epidemiological details of Andes virus (ANDV) transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and during prior reported outbreaks with confirmed person-to-person spread in Argentina, which, together, suggest aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of transmission of ANDV between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissible environmental settings.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

papers.title: Hantavirus: An Emerging Global Zoonotic Threat—From Molecular Basis to Clinical Management and Public Health Perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic viral disease caused by hantaviruses of the family Hantaviridae, primarily transmitted to humans through exposure to infected rodent urine, feces, saliva, or contaminated aerosols. The disease presents mainly in two clinical forms: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), prevalent in Asia and Europe, and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS)/Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas. The historical recognition of hantavirus began during the Korean War (1950–1953), when thousands of soldiers developed Korean hemorrhagic fever. In 1978, Ho-Wang Lee isolated the Hantaan virus from Apodemus agrarius, marking a major scientific breakthrough. Subsequent decades witnessed the identification of multiple hantavirus species, including Seoul, Puumala, Dobrava-Belgrade, Sin Nombre, and Andes viruses, each associated with distinct rodent reservoirs and clinical manifestations. A major epidemiological milestone occurred in 1993 with the outbreak of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome in the Four Corners region of the United States, leading to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus. Increasing urbanization, climate change, deforestation, and closer human–rodent interactions have contributed to the global emergence of hantavirus infections in the 21st century. Advances in molecular diagnostics, including reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and serological testing, have enhanced disease surveillance and early diagnosis. This review highlights the historical evolution, epidemiology, transmission, and growing public health significance of hantavirus infection worldwide. Keywords: Hantavirus infection; Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS); Hantavirus Pulmonary

papers.full_text: Review Article 490 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) Hantavirus Infection as an Emerging Global Zoonotic Threat: From Molecular Basis to Clinical Management and Public Health Perspectives 1Mohd Abid*, 2Ghulam Muhiyuddin, 3Saqib Tanveer, 3Mohd Asif 1Department of Pharmacology, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India 2Department of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India 3Department of Pharmaceutics, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India Keywords Abstract Hantavirus; Orthohantavirus; HFRS; HPS; HCPS; Zoonotic disease. Hantavirus infection is a rodent-associated zoonosis caused predominantly by members of the genus Orthohantavirus and characterized by substantial geographic, ecological, and clinical heterogeneity. Human disease ranges from nonspecific febrile illness to two severe syndromic presentations: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary or cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas. Disease severity is driven by the interaction of viral factors, endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular permeability, platelet abnormalities, and coordinated innate and adaptive immune responses rather than by extensive direct cytolysis alone. This review integrates current knowledge of hantavirus taxonomy, genome organization, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, clinical progression, laboratory diagnosis, supportive and antiviral management, prevention, vaccine development, and emerging surveillance approaches. Particular attention is given to the 2026 Andes hantavirus cluster associated with the MV Hondius expedition cruise, which demonstrated limited secondary person-to-person transmission and the importance of international contact tracing. Advances in molecular surveillance, genomics, rapid diagnostics, immunotherapeutic strategies, and One Health preparedness are discussed alongside persistent barriers, including restricted therapeutic options, limited cross-protective vaccines, diagnostic delays, and ecological unpredictability. An integrated prevention and response framework that connects rodent ecology, clinical recognition, laboratory capacity, intensive care, and public-health surveillance remains essential for reducing hantavirus-associated morbidity and mortality. *Corresponding Author: Dr. Mohd Abid (fromabid@yahoo.com) ORCID ID: 0000-0002-9610-2057 Article Info Received: 19 May 2026, Received in revised form: 08 October 2026, Accepted: 08 October 2026, Available online: 10 October 2026; Volume: 2; Issue: 3; Pages: 490-510. ISSN: 3049-2955/The authors © 2026, under exclusive license to the Sprout Publication DOI: 10.63785/cpr.2026.2.3.490510 Review Article 491 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) 1. Introduction Hantavirus infection is a zoonotic disease associated primarily with small mammals and remains an important cause of severe acute febrile illness in regions where pathogenic orthohantaviruses circulate. Human infection is usually acquired through contact with an infected reservoir host or through inhalation of virus-containing material generated from rodent urine, feces, saliva, or nesting material. The epidemiology is highly focal because individual viral lineages are often maintained within particular reservoir species, and human risk therefore changes with habitat, rodent density, occupational exposure, seasonality, land use, and human behavior. The two major clinical syndromes are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary or cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS), which differ in the dominant organs involved but share important pathophysiological features centered on vascular permeability and dysregulated host responses [1]. The modern understanding of hantavirus disease has evolved from outbreak recognition to molecular epidemiology and systems-level surveillance. The discovery of Hantaan virus in the late twentieth century established the rodent reservoir connection, while the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States and identification of Sin Nombre virus established HPS as a distinct severe clinical entity in the Americas. Subsequent studies demonstrated extensive viral and ecological diversity, including the ability of Andes virus to undergo limited person-to- person transmission under conditions of close and prolonged exposure. Current taxonomy places the mammalian human-pathogenic viruses within the family Hantaviridae, subfamily Mammantavirinae, and genus Orthohantavirus, reflecting a broader understanding of hantavirid diversity than the older classification systems used in many clinical reviews [2]. Despite improved laboratory diagnostics and supportive critical care, hantavirus infection remains difficult to manage because the clinical deterioration of severe disease can be rapid and no globally licensed curative antiviral therapy is available. This review therefore examines the disease as an integrated ecological, virological, clinical, and public-health problem. Particular emphasis is placed on mechanisms that connect viral entry and replication with endothelial dysfunction, organ-specific syndromes, diagnostic decision-making, treatment limitations, vaccine development, and the growing importance of genomic and One Health surveillance [3]. 2. Historical Background and Discovery 2.1 Early Recognition and the Korean Hemorrhagic Fever Era The clinical syndrome now recognized as HFRS drew major international attention during the Korean War, when thousands of United Nations soldiers developed an acute febrile illness accompanied by renal dysfunction, hemorrhagic manifestations, hypotension, and shock [4]. The disease was initially described as Korean hemorrhagic fever, and the geographic association with the Hantaan River became an important clue to its natural history. Although the outbreak produced a strong epidemiological signal, the etiological agent remained elusive for decades because the disease was associated with an environmentally acquired infection that did not fit the conventional models of human-to-human viral transmission [5]. A decisive breakthrough came in 1978 when Ho-Wang Lee and colleagues isolated the etiological virus from the striped field mouse, Apodemus agrarius, in the region of the Hantaan River. This finding established a durable link between pathogenic hantaviruses and persistent infection in rodent hosts and created the basis for ecological surveillance. The discovery also clarified why human disease was geographically patterned and why rodent abundance, habitat disturbance, and occupational exposure could alter risk without requiring sustained transmission between people [6]. 2.2 Expansion of Hantavirus Discovery and Classification Following the identification of Hantaan virus, related viruses were recognized in multiple regions and linked to distinct reservoir hosts. Seoul virus was associated with commensal rats and demonstrated a distribution compatible with urban exposure, whereas Puumala virus became closely associated with nephropathia epidemica, a comparatively milder form of HFRS in northern and central Europe. Dobrava-associated disease was recognized as another severe HFRS phenotype in parts of southeastern Europe. The expanding catalogue showed that hantavirus ecology is structured by host-virus relationships rather than by geography alone [7]. The current taxonomic framework further reflects this diversity. ICTV classifies Hantaviridae within the class Bunyaviricetes and order Elliovirales; mammalian hantaviruses are distributed across several genera, while human disease is associated with Orthohantavirus. The genome architecture is conserved across the family, but viral sequence Review Article 492 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) variation, glycoprotein properties, reservoir adaptation, and host-response differences contribute to species-specific ecological and clinical phenotypes. This modern classification is important because older descriptions based only on a few rodent-borne viruses can underestimate the breadth of hantavirid diversity [8]. 2.3 Emergence of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome In 1993, an outbreak in the Four Corners region of the United States was characterized by rapidly progressive respiratory failure in previously healthy individuals. Investigation identified a previously unrecognized hantavirus that was subsequently named Sin Nombre virus and traced to the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. The event established HPS as a severe pulmonary syndrome distinct from the renal- predominant disease recognized in Eurasia. It also demonstrated the value of integrating clinical observation, epidemiology, molecular virology, and wildlife investigation during an unexplained outbreak [9]. The discovery of Andes virus and subsequent South American outbreaks provided additional insight into hantavirus transmission. Unlike most pathogenic hantaviruses, Andes virus has repeatedly been associated with limited human-to-human transmission among close contacts. This phenotype does not represent sustained community transmission; rather, it highlights a specific transmission capability that becomes epidemiologically relevant when close contact occurs during the period of high clinical infectivity [10]. 2.4 Hantavirus in the Twenty-First Century Twenty-first-century hantavirus surveillance increasingly recognizes that emergence is shaped by interactions among ecological change, host population dynamics, climate variability, land-use change, mobility, and diagnostic capacity. Urbanization may increase contact with commensal rodents, while deforestation and agricultural expansion can alter wildlife interfaces. Climate-related changes can influence rodent population abundance and movement in some ecosystems, but the relationship is nonlinear and depends on local precipitation, food availability, predator dynamics, and habitat structure. Consequently, environmental change should be viewed as a set of modifiers of transmission opportunity rather than as a single causal driver [11]. A particularly instructive recent event occurred in 2026 in association with the MV Hondius expedition cruise. The outbreak was identified after severe respiratory illness among passengers and crew and was attributed to Andes virus. By 2 July 2026, WHO reported 13 linked cases, including 12 laboratory- confirmed cases and one probable case, with three deaths. All identified cases were among people who had travelled on the vessel. The investigation supported a point-source introduction followed by limited secondary person-to-person transmission, and WHO reported that the outbreak was contained with no further related transmission expected. The event illustrates how a pathogen that ordinarily depends on zoonotic exposure can create a short-lived international public-health challenge when infected individuals enter a confined travel setting [12]. 3. Virology and Molecular Characteristics 3.1 Taxonomy and Virion Architecture Hantaviridae is a diverse family of enveloped negative- sense RNA viruses. The current ICTV framework places the family in the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Bunyaviricetes, and order Elliovirales. Mammalian hantavirids occur in several genera, but the human pathogenic viruses currently recognized belong to Orthohantavirus. The virion is generally pleomorphic and approximately 80–160 nm in diameter, with an envelope containing the Gn and Gc glycoproteins arranged as surface spikes. These glycoproteins mediate attachment, entry, and important antigenic interactions with the host immune system [13]. The association of specific orthohantaviruses with particular rodent or other small-mammal reservoirs is a defining ecological feature. Reservoir infection is generally persistent and clinically inapparent, suggesting long-term host adaptation. In humans, however, the outcome can range from mild or nonspecific illness to rapidly progressive HFRS or HCPS. The disconnect between apparently benign reservoir infection and severe human disease emphasizes that pathogenicity depends on both viral properties and the context of spillover into an immunologically different host [14]. 3.2 Genome Organization and Viral Proteins Orthohantaviruses possess a tripartite, negative-sense RNA genome comprising small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, which binds genomic RNA and participates in ribonucleoprotein organization and replication. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is processed into Gn and Gc, the principal envelope proteins. The L segment encodes the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which carries out transcription and replication of the segmented genome. Viral mRNAs are capped but not polyadenylated, and cap-snatching from host cellular mRNAs contributes to efficient transcription [15]. Review Article 493 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) The tripartite architecture is biologically consequential because replication depends on coordinated packaging and synthesis of three distinct RNA segments. Segment reassortment and sequence variation can alter viral phenotype and complicate molecularsurveillance. At the same time, conserved structural and enzymatic functions provide targets for diagnostic assay design, antibody development, antiviral screening, and vaccine engineering. Understanding the relationships among N, Gn/Gc, and polymerase functions therefore remains central to translating virological knowledge into clinical and public-health applications [16]. 3.3 Viral Entry, Replication, and Cellular Tropism Hantavirus attachment and entry involve interactions between viral glycoproteins and host-cell receptors, with beta-3 integrins representing an important component of the receptor biology described for pathogenic hantaviruses. Endothelial cells are a major cellular target, yet infection of these cells does not typically produce the extensive direct cytolysis that characterizes some other viral diseases. Instead, hantavirus replication occurs in the setting of altered endothelial signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, junctional integrity, platelet interactions, and inflammatory mediator release. This helps explain why dramatic vascular leakage can coexist with relatively limited structural destruction of the endothelial monolayer [17]. After entry, the negative-sense RNA genome must be transcribed by the viral polymerase before viral proteins can be produced. Newly synthesized ribonucleoprotein complexes and glycoproteins are assembled through coordinated intracellular trafficking, followed by budding and release of progeny virions. The precise contribution of individual host pathways to severe disease continues to be investigated, but current models emphasize that pathogenicity emerges from the combination of viral replication, host-cell signaling, complement and coagulation pathways, platelet-endothelial interactions, and innate and adaptive immune responses [18]. 4. Reservoirs and Transmission 4.1 Reservoir Ecology Rodents constitute the principal reservoir hosts for the orthohantaviruses that cause human disease, with many viral lineages showing a close association with particular host species. Examples include Apodemus species for Hantaan virus, Rattus species for Seoul virus, bank voles for Puumala virus, and Peromyscus maniculatus for Sin Nombre virus. Andes virus is associated with sigmodontine rodents in South America. Reservoir specificity helps shape geographic distribution and also means that changes in host abundance or habitat can alter human exposure even when the virus itself has not changed [19]. Reservoir surveillance is therefore more informative when it integrates virological detection with ecological measurements such as rodent density, reproductive cycles, vegetation, food availability, habitat fragmentation, and human land use. From a One Health perspective, spillover should be understood as the outcome of a connected system involving reservoir competence, environmental contamination, human behavior, and access to health services [20]. 4.2 Routes of Transmission to Humans Most human infections result from exposure to infectious rodent excreta or contaminated environmental material. Transmission may also occur when contaminated material contacts mucous membranes or broken skin. Rodent bites and scratches are possible but are less common routes. Ingestion of contaminated food or water is biologically plausible but is less clearly established than inhalational or direct mucosal exposure [21]. The incubation period is variable and generally spans approximately one to eight weeks, depending on the virus and exposure context. Because the early clinical syndrome is nonspecific, a history of rodent exposure often provides the epidemiological clue that makes targeted laboratory testing appropriate. Exposure assessment should therefore include home and workplace conditions, cleaning activities, agricultural or forestry work, travel to endemic regions, and direct contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated materials [22]. 4.3 Human-to-Human Transmission Person-to-person transmission is not a general feature of hantavirus infection. The best-established example is Andes virus, for which limited transmission has been documented among household members, intimate contacts, and healthcare-associated close contacts. Available observations indicate that prolonged, close contact during the early clinical phase is particularly relevant. Other pathogenic hantaviruses have not demonstrated comparable sustained…

full_text_sections.full_text: Review Article 490 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) Hantavirus Infection as an Emerging Global Zoonotic Threat: From Molecular Basis to Clinical Management and Public Health Perspectives 1Mohd Abid*, 2Ghulam Muhiyuddin, 3Saqib Tanveer, 3Mohd Asif 1Department of Pharmacology, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India 2Department of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India 3Department of Pharmaceutics, JIT, Faculty of Pharmacy, Jahangirabaad, Barabanki, 225203, Uttar Pradesh, India Keywords Abstract Hantavirus; Orthohantavirus; HFRS; HPS; HCPS; Zoonotic disease. Hantavirus infection is a rodent-associated zoonosis caused predominantly by members of the genus Orthohantavirus and characterized by substantial geographic, ecological, and clinical heterogeneity. Human disease ranges from nonspecific febrile illness to two severe syndromic presentations: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary or cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas. Disease severity is driven by the interaction of viral factors, endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular permeability, platelet abnormalities, and coordinated innate and adaptive immune responses rather than by extensive direct cytolysis alone. This review integrates current knowledge of hantavirus taxonomy, genome organization, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, clinical progression, laboratory diagnosis, supportive and antiviral management, prevention, vaccine development, and emerging surveillance approaches. Particular attention is given to the 2026 Andes hantavirus cluster associated with the MV Hondius expedition cruise, which demonstrated limited secondary person-to-person transmission and the importance of international contact tracing. Advances in molecular surveillance, genomics, rapid diagnostics, immunotherapeutic strategies, and One Health preparedness are discussed alongside persistent barriers, including restricted therapeutic options, limited cross-protective vaccines, diagnostic delays, and ecological unpredictability. An integrated prevention and response framework that connects rodent ecology, clinical recognition, laboratory capacity, intensive care, and public-health surveillance remains essential for reducing hantavirus-associated morbidity and mortality. *Corresponding Author: Dr. Mohd Abid (fromabid@yahoo.com) ORCID ID: 0000-0002-9610-2057 Article Info Received: 19 May 2026, Received in revised form: 08 October 2026, Accepted: 08 October 2026, Available online: 10 October 2026; Volume: 2; Issue: 3; Pages: 490-510. ISSN: 3049-2955/The authors © 2026, under exclusive license to the Sprout Publication DOI: 10.63785/cpr.2026.2.3.490510 Review Article 491 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) 1. Introduction Hantavirus infection is a zoonotic disease associated primarily with small mammals and remains an important cause of severe acute febrile illness in regions where pathogenic orthohantaviruses circulate. Human infection is usually acquired through contact with an infected reservoir host or through inhalation of virus-containing material generated from rodent urine, feces, saliva, or nesting material. The epidemiology is highly focal because individual viral lineages are often maintained within particular reservoir species, and human risk therefore changes with habitat, rodent density, occupational exposure, seasonality, land use, and human behavior. The two major clinical syndromes are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary or cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS), which differ in the dominant organs involved but share important pathophysiological features centered on vascular permeability and dysregulated host responses [1]. The modern understanding of hantavirus disease has evolved from outbreak recognition to molecular epidemiology and systems-level surveillance. The discovery of Hantaan virus in the late twentieth century established the rodent reservoir connection, while the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States and identification of Sin Nombre virus established HPS as a distinct severe clinical entity in the Americas. Subsequent studies demonstrated extensive viral and ecological diversity, including the ability of Andes virus to undergo limited person-to- person transmission under conditions of close and prolonged exposure. Current taxonomy places the mammalian human-pathogenic viruses within the family Hantaviridae, subfamily Mammantavirinae, and genus Orthohantavirus, reflecting a broader understanding of hantavirid diversity than the older classification systems used in many clinical reviews [2]. Despite improved laboratory diagnostics and supportive critical care, hantavirus infection remains difficult to manage because the clinical deterioration of severe disease can be rapid and no globally licensed curative antiviral therapy is available. This review therefore examines the disease as an integrated ecological, virological, clinical, and public-health problem. Particular emphasis is placed on mechanisms that connect viral entry and replication with endothelial dysfunction, organ-specific syndromes, diagnostic decision-making, treatment limitations, vaccine development, and the growing importance of genomic and One Health surveillance [3]. 2. Historical Background and Discovery 2.1 Early Recognition and the Korean Hemorrhagic Fever Era The clinical syndrome now recognized as HFRS drew major international attention during the Korean War, when thousands of United Nations soldiers developed an acute febrile illness accompanied by renal dysfunction, hemorrhagic manifestations, hypotension, and shock [4]. The disease was initially described as Korean hemorrhagic fever, and the geographic association with the Hantaan River became an important clue to its natural history. Although the outbreak produced a strong epidemiological signal, the etiological agent remained elusive for decades because the disease was associated with an environmentally acquired infection that did not fit the conventional models of human-to-human viral transmission [5]. A decisive breakthrough came in 1978 when Ho-Wang Lee and colleagues isolated the etiological virus from the striped field mouse, Apodemus agrarius, in the region of the Hantaan River. This finding established a durable link between pathogenic hantaviruses and persistent infection in rodent hosts and created the basis for ecological surveillance. The discovery also clarified why human disease was geographically patterned and why rodent abundance, habitat disturbance, and occupational exposure could alter risk without requiring sustained transmission between people [6]. 2.2 Expansion of Hantavirus Discovery and Classification Following the identification of Hantaan virus, related viruses were recognized in multiple regions and linked to distinct reservoir hosts. Seoul virus was associated with commensal rats and demonstrated a distribution compatible with urban exposure, whereas Puumala virus became closely associated with nephropathia epidemica, a comparatively milder form of HFRS in northern and central Europe. Dobrava-associated disease was recognized as another severe HFRS phenotype in parts of southeastern Europe. The expanding catalogue showed that hantavirus ecology is structured by host-virus relationships rather than by geography alone [7]. The current taxonomic framework further reflects this diversity. ICTV classifies Hantaviridae within the class Bunyaviricetes and order Elliovirales; mammalian hantaviruses are distributed across several genera, while human disease is associated with Orthohantavirus. papers.title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. METHODS: Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. FINDINGS: Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. INTERPRETATION: Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. FUNDING: Defense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

papers.title: Dual-Target Inhibition of Puumala Virus Entry Glycoproteins Gn and Gc by Moringa oleifera -Derived Phytochemicals: An Integrated Computational Study
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), a member of the Orthohantavirus genus, causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate type of hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, yet no approved antiviral therapy is currently available. Viral entry is initiated by the coordinated actions of the attachment glycoprotein Gn and fusion glycoprotein Gc, making simultaneous inhibition of these proteins an attractive antiviral strategy. Here, we employed a combined computational workflow to identify dual-target inhibitors of PUUV entry glycoproteins from Moringa oleifera phytochemicals. 72 phytochemicals were retrieved and docked by molecular docking to identify high-affinity binders, while he top-ranked compounds were subsequently evaluated for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behavior, toxicity, and predicted biological activities to assess their therapeutic suitability. Complex stability and binding mechanisms were further investigated through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations. Quercetin and kaempferol showed the lowest binding energies toward Gn (−9.8 and −9.7 kcal/mol) and Gc (−10.4 and −10.0 kcal/mol), respectively. Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine labo- ratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corre- sponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5). Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to b3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation dis- turbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9). Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechan- ical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes. In recent years, research on early warning of severe HFRS has advanced considerably across multiple levels, encompassing bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging novel biomarkers. In this review, we comprehensively synthesize progress in the aforementioned areas and evaluate the predictive performance and translational potential of various bio- markers. We also discuss current challenges and future perspec- tives, with the aim of establishing an evidence base for early identification and precise management of severe HFRS. 2 Clinically accessible warning systems for early risk stratification Clinically accessible warning systems including bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters are the most important indicators for predicting severe HFRS. This section reviews the available evidence on bedside signs and standard laboratory tests for predicting severe HFRS. The goal is to provide a practical frame- work for early risk assessment. 2.1 Bedside signs of severe HFRS prediction Bedside signs offer unique discriminative value for early risk stratification in HFRS, particularly in the absence of laboratory data. The 2021 Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Treatment of HFRS identifies several key warning indicators for severe cases. These include a history of travel to endemic areas or contact with rodents and their excreta within two months prior to onset, high fever (temperature >40 °C or febrile duration exceeding one week), severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as intense nausea and vomiting, psychiatric disturbances including agitation or delirium, marked conjunctival edema, and obvious bleeding tendency (10). Regarding imaging findings, a retrospective analysis by Huang et al. of 191 patients with HFRS in southwestern China demonstrated that pleural effusion was an independent risk factor for progression to severe HFRS. Patients with pleural effusion had a 4.49-fold higher risk of severe progression compared to those without it, suggesting that this sign may reflect more extensive capillary leakage and systemic inflammation (14). The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score also has shown significant value in predicting severe HFRS. Ma and colleagues conducted a multicenter study of 551 HFRS patients in Hubei Province. They demonstrated that an admission qSOFA score of 2 or higher was an independent risk factor for 30-day mortality. The qSOFA score is defined as meeting any two of the following criteria: respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, or altered mental status. This finding suggests that the qSOFA score, without reliance on any laboratory tests, can serve as a rapid triage tool for early identification of high- risk HFRS patients and for determining the need for intensive care unit admission (19). Notably, the early warning indicators for severe HFRS vary across different age groups. Researchers at Tangdu Hospital have conducted stratified warning analyses for both older adults and children (20, 21). In the older-adult cohort (≥60 years), Li et al. reviewed 146 cases and identified several early warning signs using multivariate logistic regression. These included chest tightness or dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, decreased urine output (UO), skin and mucosal hemorrhage, and phase overlap (disease course span- ning two or more typical phases). These findings suggest that assessment of older adults with HFRS should focus more on cardiopulmonary function, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal perfu- sion, coagulation status, and disease progression patterns (20). In the pediatric cohort (<16 years), the same group analyzed 103 cases. They found that conjunctival edema, hypotensive shock, and elevated serum creatinine (Cr) were key early warning indicators. This suggests that assessment in children should focus more on fluid extravasation, circulatory status, and early renal changes. Taken together, risk assessment should combine exposure history, consensus-based warning signs, bedside scores, and age-specific findings (21). Li et al. 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1986264 Frontiers in Immunology frontiersin.org 02 2.2 Routine laboratory parameters for early warning of severe HFRS 2.2.1 Blood cell indices and inflammatory markers Blood count and routine inflammatory markers are the most accessible laboratory indicators for evaluating the systemic host response in HFRS. Markedly elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and severely reduced platelet count (PLT) have long been recog- nized as warning signs for HFRS severity (11, 22). The 2021 Expert Consensus has established WBC >30 × 109/L and PLT <20 × 109/L as definitive severity warning thresholds (10). This pattern has been consistently confirmed by multiple retrospective cohort studies from various regions. Yang et al. analyzed 109 HFRS cases in central China and found that the median WBC in the severe group (25.2 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the mild group (12.6 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the mild group (54 × 109/L) (12). Chen et al. further examined the association between these two indicators and adverse outcomes in a cohort of 395 HFRS patients in northwestern China. The results showed that the median WBC in the non-survivor group (23.19 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the survivor group (13.29 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the survivor group (41 × 109/L) (23). Platelet distribution width (PDW) may provide infor- mation on platelet activation and function beyond that conveyed by PLT alone. Fan et al. studied 260 HFRS patients and found that PDW on the first day of admission increased significantly with disease severity. Of note, in critically ill patients, the association between PDW and prognosis was reversed, with non-survivors exhibiting lower PDW than survivors. This reversal may reflect exhausted marrow hematopoietic compensation, where declining PDW portends worse outcomes (24). The neutrophil-to-red blood cell ratio (NRR) and neutrophil- to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), as simple readouts of systemic inflam- mation, have demonstrated predictive value across multiple viral species. Xiao et al. analyzed 342 HTNV-HFRS cases in Xi’an and found that NRR was significantly elevated in the severe/critical group, with optimal discriminative performance for severity grad- ing, whereas NLR was significantly elevated in the non-survivor group, with optimal performance for 28-day all-cause mortality prediction. Both markers are accessible at the bedside, with NRR more suitable for early severity stratification and NLR better aligned with mortality risk assessment (25). In PUUV infection, Nusshag et al. analyzed 32 PUUV-infected patients in Germany and showed that peak NLR was significantly elevated in severe patients with hospitalization exceeding five days, suggesting that systemic neu- trophil-lymphocyte imbalance is an important accompanying fea- ture of PUUV severity (26). Procalcitonin (PCT), as an indicator reflecting the severity of infection and inflammation, has shown predictive value across multiple independent studies. Duan et al. found that serum PCT level at emergency department admission was an independent risk factor for severe progression in HFRS patients, with the median PCT in the severe group significantly higher than in the mild group (8.12 vs. 1.39 ng/mL); an admission PCT exceeding 2.97 ng/mL demonstrated good predictive value for severity, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.862, and a sensitivity of 88.0% (27). Chen et al. found in 272 HFRS patients that admission PCT levels increased significantly with disease severity, with an AUC of 0.792 for predicting 28-day survival/ death at an optimal cutoff of 2.28 ng/mL, outperforming WBC (AUC 0.769) (28). Che et al. further confirmed in a retrospective study of 373 HFRS patients that the median admission PCT in the severe group was significantly higher than in the mild group (3.8 vs. 1.3 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.824 for predicting severity; PCT was also significantly higher in non-survivors than in survivors (3.6 vs. 1.7 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.737 for predicting hospital mortality (7). Huang et al. confirmed in a retrospective cohort of 191 HFRS patients in southwestern China that PCT was an independent risk factor for severe progression, with each 1 ng/mL increase in PCT associated with approximately 33% higher odds of developing severe disease (14). Yu et al. also confirmed in a cohort of 384 HFRS patients that PCT was significantly higher in the severe/ critical group than in the mild/moderate group, with multivariate logistic regression confirming elevated PCT as an independent predictor of severe progression (29). These results indicate that PCT is a useful marker for assessing both disease severity and short- term mortality in HFRS, and may help identify high-risk pa- tients early. Unlike PCT, C-reactive protein (CRP) showed limited inde- pendent value for HFRS severity prediction. Che et al. studied 373 HFRS patients and found that admission CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (median 42.1 vs. 29.5 mg/L). However, its AUC for severity prediction was only 0.614, far below that of PCT (0.824) (7). Yang et al. also found that although the median CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (51.0 vs. 30.9 mg/L), CRP was deemed to lack independent incremental value during least absolute shrink- age and selection operator (LASSO) regression variable selection and was therefore not included in the final prediction model (12). Chen et al. further confirmed in 272 HFRS patients that admission CRP was elevated across all severity grades (mean approximately 30.1 to 33.96 mg/L for each group), with no statistically significant difference among the four groups, indicating that CRP does not exhibit a gradient change with disease severity. However, CRP retains potential utility in assessing secondary bacterial infection: the median CRP in the infected group was significantly higher than in the non-infected group (43.2 vs. 26.4 mg/L, p < 0.001), with an AUC of 0.588 for predicting secondary bacterial infection (p = 0.005). Although this represents moderate-to-weak performance, it is statistically significant, whereas PCT showed no discriminative capacity in this setting (28). Therefore, CRP is more suitable as an auxiliary marker for bacterial infection rather than an independent predictor of HFRS severity. The predictive role of serum albumin (ALB) and hemoglobin (Hb) remains controversial. The 2021 Expert Consensus lists serum ALB below 15 g/L as a severity warning indicator (10). Huang et al. reported that the median admission ALB was significantly lower in the severe group than in the mild group (25.45 vs. 29.80 g/L) on univariate analysis. Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to b3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators, including bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction, renal injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation.
analysis.current_state: Clinically accessible indicators such as fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, bleeding, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin consistently predict severity and mortality, while immunological profiles reveal cytokine imbalance and impaired adaptive responses.
analysis.gaps: Challenges persist in external validation and clinical translation of these indicators, limiting their routine use.
analysis.future_research: Future work should establish standardized, multicenter‑validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen mainly distributed in East Asia and causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans while persisting asymptomatically in rodent reservoirs.
analysis.methods: The study used an integrated bioinformatics workflow to identify early‑stage HTNV host interaction factors, screen natural compounds from the HERB database, and predict therapeutic mechanisms.
analysis.results: Core up‑regulated genes CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were identified; six candidate natural compounds were retrieved, with quercetin highlighted as the most promising due to favorable ADMET predictions; quercetin showed low cytotoxicity at 3.9–7.8 µM in HEK293T cells, increased viability, reduced BCL2, MAPK3 and TNF transcription, and docked favorably to HTNV RdRp (contacting Lys884 and Arg892).
analysis.contribution: The work proposes quercetin as a hypothesis‑generating computational candidate to modulate HTNV‑related host responses and offers a mechanistic framework that could aid One Health‑based surveillance and control strategies.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on abstract‑level computational and in‑silico analyses; experimental validation is pending and the abstract does not provide detailed methods or data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen in East Asia that causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans while remaining asymptomatic in rodents. Results: CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were up‑regulated; six natural compounds were retrieved, with quercetin most promising, showing low cytotoxicity at 3.9–7.8 µM, increased cell viability, reduced BCL2/MAPK3/TNF transcription, and favorable docking to HTNV RdRp (Lys884, Arg892). Contribution: The study proposes quercetin as a hypothesis‑generating candidate to modulate HTNV host responses, supporting One Health surveillance and control. papers.title_zh: 预测槲皮素作为HTNV相关宿主反应潜在调节剂:基于基线药理特征的综合计算研究

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒 (HTNV) 是一种主要分布于东亚的啮齿类传播的动物源性病原体,导致人类严重的肾综合征出血热,同时在啮齿类宿主中无症状持续存在。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用集成生物信息学工作流程,识别早期 HTNV 主机相互作用因子,筛选 HERB 数据库中的天然化合物,并预测治疗机制。
analysis_zh.results: 识别出核心上调基因 CXCL10、STAT1 和 IL10;检索到六种候选天然化合物,其中槲皮素因 ADMET 预测优异而被突出为最有前景的;槲皮素在 3.9–7.8 μM 的 HEK293T 细胞中显示低细胞毒性,提升细胞存活率,降低 BCL2、MAPK3 和 TNF 的转录水平,并与 HTNV RdRp 有良好结合(接触 Lys884 和 Arg892)。
