papers.title: Integrated immunoinformatics and molecular dynamics approaches reveal a promising multi-epitope vaccine against hantavirus.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), with substantial global morbidity and mortality. No universally approved human vaccine exists, making a safe, effective vaccine a public health priority. An immunoinformatics strategy was used to design a multi-epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor (GP_HANTL) of Hantaan orthohantavirus. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and B-cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC-binding affinity, and population coverage. Selected epitopes were joined with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and fused to a β-defensin adjuvant. The construct was evaluated by physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization, and in silico cloning. The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, with 99.24% global population coverage. Structural validation showed 95% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82. Molecular docking produced a favorable ClusPro score (- 1273.6) for the selected MEVC-TLR4 complex. Immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses, including elevated antibodies, memory B cells, and CTL/HTL activation. Codon optimization yielded a CAI of 0.94, supporting efficient Escherichia coli expression. A 100-ns MD simulation showed substantial conformational adaptation of the MEVC while TLR4 remained comparatively stable; accompanying Rg and SASA trends indicated that the MEVC adopted a more compact state during the trajectory. The proposed MEVC demonstrated favorable predicted immunogenicity, favorable structural characteristics, broad population coverage, and favorable expression characteristics. These findings support experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against Hantavirus infection. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00782-6.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome, with substantial global morbidity and mortality; no universally approved human vaccine exists, making vaccine development a public‑health priority.
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics pipeline was applied to design a multi‑epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor of Hantaan orthohantavirus, predicting CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes, screening for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC affinity and population coverage, linking epitopes with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and a β‑defensin adjuvant, and evaluating the construct via physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, docking, molecular dynamics, immune simulation, codon optimization and in‑silico cloning.
analysis.results: The final MEVC contains 10 CTL, 10 HTL and 5 B‑cell epitopes with 99.24% global population coverage; structural validation shows 95% residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82; docking to TLR4 yields a ClusPro score of –1273.6; immune simulations predict robust humoral and cellular responses; codon optimization gives a CAI of 0.94; a 100‑ns MD simulation shows the MEVC adopting a more compact state (decreasing Rg and SASA) while TLR4 remains stable.
analysis.contribution: The in‑silico MEVC demonstrates favorable predicted immunogenicity, structural stability, broad population coverage and expression potential, providing a basis for experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against hantavirus infection.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on computational analyses; no experimental validation is reported and the evidence is limited to the abstract.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes severe disease and lacks an approved human vaccine, creating a public‑health need. Methods: An immunoinformatics workflow designed a multi‑epitope vaccine targeting the Hantaan virus glycoprotein, predicting CTL, HTL and B‑cell epitopes, linking them with specific linkers and a β‑defensin adjuvant, and evaluating the construct through physicochemical, structural, docking, MD, immune simulation, codon optimization and cloning analyses. Results: The construct includes 10 CTL, 10 HTL and 5 B‑cell epitopes covering 99.24% of the global population; 95% of residues are in favored Ramachandran regions (ERRAT 82); docking to TLR4 yields a ClusPro score of –1273.6; immune simulation predicts strong humoral and cellular responses; codon optimization gives a CAI of 0.94; MD shows the vaccine becoming more compact while TLR4 stays stable. Contribution: The predicted vaccine shows favorable immunogenicity, stability, broad coverage and expression potential, supporting further experimental work. Limitations: Results are purely computational; no experimental validation is presented and only the abstract is available.

papers.title_zh: 综合免疫信息学与分子动力学方法揭示针对 汉坦病毒 的有前景的多表位疫苗。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是一种啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒肺综合征,在全球造成显著的发病率和死亡率;目前尚无普遍认可的人用疫苗,使疫苗研发成为公共卫生重点。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用免疫信息学流程设计针对汉滩病毒 正汉坦病毒 糖蛋白前体的多表位疫苗构建体(MEVC),预测细胞毒性T细胞(CTL)、辅助性T细胞(HTL)和B细胞表位,筛选抗原性、免疫原性、MHC亲和力和人群覆盖率,使用EAAAK、AAY、GPGPG、KK 链接子以及β-防御素佐剂连接表位,并通过理化特性分析、结构建模、对接、分子动力学、免疫模拟、密码子优化和体外克隆对构建体进行评估。
analysis_zh.results: 最终MEVC包含10个CTL、10个HTL和5个B细胞表位,覆盖全球人群99.24%;结构验证显示95%的残基位于Favored Ramachandran区,ERRAT得分为82;与TLR4对接的ClusPro得分为‐1273.6;免疫模拟预测产生强烈的体液和细胞免疫应答;密码子优化后CAI为0.94;100 ns的MD模拟显示MEVC趋于更紧凑状态(Rg和SASA下降),而TLR4保持稳定。

papers.title: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations
papers.abstract: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository.

papers.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted Records The extraction sheets are not edited after extraction. Corrections are listed in tables in the repository, each with its source in the paper: 3,243 corrections to individual values, 331 deleted rows and 316 re-extracted rows. The pipeline downloads the sheets and applies the corrections to the downloaded copy. It stops if a value in a sheet no longer matches the value a correction expects, so a correction cannot silently overwrite a later change. 3.2.2 Metadata Consolidation Raw extractions are aggregated to consolidate citation metadata and establish unique identifiers for all studies, hosts, pathogens, and sequences. Because historical literature reports temporal data in highly variable formats (e.g., specific days, month-year, multi-year spans), a parsing function was developed to translate verbatim event dates into standardised start_date and end_date bounds, generating a consistent temporal_resolution flag for every record. 3.2.3 Taxonomic and Spatial Resolution Host taxonomy is resolved via the taxize package (Chamberlain et al. 2020), querying the GBIF API to append standardised hierarchies (Species through Class) and persistent taxonID keys (Chamberlain et al. 2026). Concurrently, geographical point data undergo validation against standard administrative boundaries. Coordinates are matched to their corresponding ISO-3166 country codes, and a spatial join against the Database of Global Administrative Areas (GADM, version 4.1) enriches each record with standardised sub- national administrative levels (adm1, adm2, adm3) relevant to the level of geographic resolution (Database of Global Administrative Areas 2022; Hijmans et al. 2024). Where a paper gave no coordinates, the named locality (a village, town or administrative unit) was located using Google Maps, Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap or the GEOnet Names Server, and coordinate_resolution_processed records the level of that locality. One study gives its sites only as GADM version 2.8 municipality identifiers (Wang et al. 2023); these records are placed at a point inside each municipality. 3.2.4 Trapping Effort To support downstream macro-ecological modelling, unstructured, free-text trapping descriptions are parsed to extract trap-night metrics, recorded in trap_nights_clean and described by trap_nights_status. Where source manuscripts reported data in tabular form listing multiple species and sampling sites, zero-detection records were extracted directly from blank or absent cells, preserving the structure of the original study design. Users should be aware that a zero-detection record in host_occurrences reflects a recorded absence within a specific sample, and should not be interpreted as ecological absence from the broader study area. 3.2.5 Pathogen and Genomic Enrichment Pathogen nomenclature undergoes parallel harmonisation against the NCBI Taxonomy database (Schoch et al. 2020). To bridge the gap between ecological sampling and molecular epidemiology, raw NCBI GenBank accession numbers extracted from the literature are passed back through the NCBI Entrez API (Sayers et al. 2024). This automated sequence enrichment downloads and parses the metadata for each accession. The host and pathogen names in each GenBank record are then compared with the names assigned in ArHa, and the differences are listed in the quality assurance report. Differences are not corrected automatically, because GenBank host metadata are often incomplete or give a synonym, an older name or a higher taxon (see Technical Validation). 3.2.6 Cross-study Duplicate Resolution Some field data were published in more than one paper and so entered ArHa more than once. After enrichment, the pipeline resolves these cases from a table of decisions in the processing scripts. Records are removed where a paper repeats data already extracted from another, merged where two papers report complementary results for the same animals, and linked as a duplicate group where the same animals are reported at different spatial or temporal breakdowns that cannot be reconciled (duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events). How the duplicates were found, and how many, is described below. 3.2.7 Quality Assurance and Schema Formatting Prior to final compilation, the pipeline generates a quality assurance report to evaluate database dimensions, coordinate validity, and taxonomic consistency. The final output is then structured into the four-tier relational schema. 3.3 Duplicate Publication of Field Data The same field data may be published more than once: a survey reported in several papers, a synthesis that consolidates earlier studies, or results reanalysed in a later paper. Where a paper does not say that its data have been published before, extraction can duplicate data. The same animals, sites and assay results then enter the database more than once, affecting subsequent counts, prevalences and ranges drawn from, in ways that cannot be seen in the data. To find such cases, each assay record was given a fingerprint of host species, pathogen, number positive, number tested and country, and pairs of studies that shared these fingerprints with overlapping sampling dates were flagged; study totals were compared in the same way. Each flagged pair was checked against both papers. Of the 44 pairs checked, 19 shared counts by chance. The rest were resolved by pre-defined rules: keep the most complete source data; where two papers report the same animals at breakdowns that cannot be merged, keep both and link them; and do not treat a review, or a second copy of the same paper, as a source. In all, 15 studies were removed entirely. Of these, 5 were one paper entered under two citation records. A further 124 host records were removed where two papers overlapped in part, and 43 host records were merged where two papers reported different assays on the same animals. Studies reporting the same animals in formats that cannot be merged are retained and linked through duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events: 6 studies in 3 groups (see Usage Notes). Each action is listed in the processing scripts and summarised in duplicate_resolution.csv. 3.4 The ArHa Database Explorer To visualise the relational data architecture and improve accessibility for the wider ecological and public health communities, the database is accompanied by the ArHa Database Explorer (https://diddrog11.shinyapps.io/arenavirus_hantavirus_app/). Built using R and Shiny (Chang et al. 2025), with a DuckDB backend (Mühleisen and Raasveldt 2025) for relational querying and Leaflet/plotly for interactive spatial and statistical visualisation (Cheng et al. 2024; Sievert 2020). Users can spatially visualise genomic sampling via the Leaflet integration, cross-filter by diagnostic modality or host taxonomy, and export subsets of the data for local modelling. 3.5 Data Records The ArHa database is released under a dual-format strategy to maximise utility and interoperability. This release holds 710 studies with sampling in 103 countries at 4,910 distinct localities (Figure 1). Sampling began between 1964 and 2021 (Figure 2). Figure 1: Sampling localities in ArHa, coloured by the resolution of the reported location. Each point is a distinct coordinate; a coordinate used at more than one resolution is shown at its most precise. The numbers in the legend are localities. Figure 2: Contents of ArHa. (a) Studies by the year in which sampling began, for the 689 of 710 studies that report a sampling date. (b) Host records by order. (c) Assay records for Arenaviridae and Hantaviridae by assay type; “Other or not reported” includes virus culture, sequencing, Western blot and pooled serology or PCR. 106 assay records for other or unrecorded virus families are not shown. Host occurrence records tend not to be individual animals. Each record gives the number of animals of one taxon recorded in one sampling session at one locality, and 14,333 records (26.3%) record that a taxon was not caught (individualCount = 0). Records are also unevenly spread across studies: the three studies with the most records, two long- term population studies and one survey of many localities, hold 52% of host_occurrences (Mariën et al. 2020; Cuypers et al. 2023; Guzzetta et al. 2017). Cuypers et al. (2023), for example, sampled 187 localities in Tanzania and reported results for 54 small mammal taxa at each, contributing 10,120 records (18.6% of host_occurrences) from 1,224 animals. Most of these records document that a taxon was not caught at a locality rather than a capture. Analyses that treat records as equivalent units, without reference to individualCount, will therefore over-weight studies of this kind relative to those that report only captures. 3.5.1 Schema Definition A primary vulnerability when archiving complex ecological sampling in flat-file formats is data expansion: forcing many-to-many relationships (e.g., multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host) into a single two-dimensional table can result in substantial record duplication. To mitigate this and ensure data integrity, the ArHa dataset is engineered as a four-tier relational database, summarised in Table 1 and Figure 3. Figure 3: The four relational tables of ArHa, their roles in the Darwin Core Archive, their keys and the number of records. Arrows run from the referenced table to the table that holds the key. Assay records link to a sampling event and, where the paper allows, to a host record; sequence records link to either a host or an assay record. Table 1: Summary of the four ArHa relational tables. full_text_sections.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted R…

papers.title: Rational Design of Candidate Hantavirus Gc Fusion Inhibitors Through Structure-Activity Relationship Analysis
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. Residues 308-320 undergo a non-uniform transition: the segments 308-311 and 318-320 preserved their internal geometry (span changes +0.4 Å and + 0.7 Å) while the central segment contracted sharply (313-317: 11.9 -> 6.1 Å). The selected pocket, bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 therefore spans a rigid anchoring region and an adjacent deformation zone. A library of approximately three million compounds was reduced to 1,041 docking-ready ligands and docked against prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity -5.35 kcal/mol). Two parent scaffolds (compounds 512 and 74) were carried into 38 analogues (SAR-v1-v20; MR-v1-v18) across a four node decomposition of the pocket. Each was redocked 10 times and assessed by DBSCAN pose clustering, a Gaussian residue contact fingerprint, an ensemble pose-drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after a short time scale relaxation (2 failed to parameterize). No significant pairwise correlations were detected among the three ranking criteria (residue-contact score versus MM/GBSA, Spearman ρ = 0.09, p = 0.59), so none was treated as decisive. SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. papers.title: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness.

INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. Despite growing research on hantavirus epidemiology, reservoir ecology, occupational exposure, and diagnostic techniques, important gaps remain in the integration of clinical laboratory preparedness and biosafety within hantavirus response systems [12]. Current international guidance emphasizes that laboratory confirmation requires appropriate serological or molecular testing, while potentially infectious specimens must be handled, packaged, transported, and processed under risk-appropriate containment conditions [1]. However, preparedness also depends on trained personnel, quality-management systems, validated procedures, referral networks, and sufficient resources. A recent Asia-Pacific assessment involving substantial participation from Philippine laboratories identified staff-training and budget limitations among the major barriers to strengthening laboratory quality and competence, indicating broader system-level constraints that may also affect preparedness for uncommon emerging pathogens [19]. These limitations are particularly relevant to hantavirus preparedness in the Philippines. In June 2026, the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine issued specific instructions for the collection, handling, packaging, transport, and referral of specimens from suspected hantavirus cases, emphasizing personnel safety, specimen integrity, coordination with designated reference laboratories, and compliance with biosafety and biosecurity standards [18]. Nevertheless, the existence of national referral guidance does not necessarily indicate that hantavirus testing and biosafety procedures are routinely implemented across hospital and clinical laboratories. Thus, limited evidence regarding decentralized diagnostic capacity, laboratory personnel competency, quality assurance, containment practices, and functional referral pathways represents an important knowledge gap. Systematically evaluating these areas is necessary to determine how effectively Philippine laboratories could recognize suspected hantavirus infections and safely manage and refer to associated clinical specimens, while drawing lessons from laboratory systems in other countries. . Therefore, this systematic review aims to evaluate diagnostic preparedness and biosafety measures for hantavirus infections in clinical laboratories, with particular consideration of their applicability to the Philippines. Specifically, it seeks to identify and compare diagnostic methods used for hantavirus detection; assess laboratory preparedness, testing capacity, quality assurance, and specimen-referral systems; evaluate biosafety measures for specimen collection, processing, transport, storage, and disposal; compare practices across countries and resource settings; identify major diagnostic and biosafety gaps; and determine evidence-based strategies that may strengthen hantavirus laboratory preparedness in the Philippines and comparable resource-limited settings. METHODOLOGY 2.1Study Design and Reporting Framework This study employed a systematic review design to identify, evaluate, and synthesize available evidence on hantavirus infection, with particular attention to epidemiology, human exposure, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, biosafety, and implications for public health and laboratory preparedness in the Philippines. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [20]. A structured approach was applied to literature identification, screening and eligibility assessment, data extraction, methodological appraisal, and evidence synthesis. The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [39] under registration number CRD420261485094. Given the heterogeneity of the included evidence in terms of study design, geographical setting, study populations, diagnostic approaches, exposure measures, and reported outcomes, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, findings were synthesized using a narrative and thematic approach, allowing evidence to be organized and interpreted across the major domains addressed by the review. 2.2 Literature Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies relevant to hantavirus infection and its epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, ecological, and public health dimensions. The principal electronic databases searched were PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Supplementary searches were undertaken through manual screening of reference lists and relevant institutional and research repositories. Grey literature and technical documents from recognized public health organizations and national agencies were also considered when they contributed directly to the objectives of the review. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and included terms related to Hantavirus, Orthohantavirus, human–rodent interaction, zoonotic transmission, occupational exposure, seroprevalence, reservoir surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, and public health. An example of the search strategy was: (Hantavirus or Orthohantavirus) and (occupational exposure or human–rodent interface or zoonotic transmission) and (seroprevalence or reservoir surveillance or public health) Search terms were modified where necessary to accommodate the indexing systems and search functions of individual databases. 2.3 Eligibility Criteria Studies were considered eligible when they provided evidence relevant to hantavirus infection or transmission, including human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical disease, laboratory diagnosis, occupational or environmental risk, rodent reservoirs, ecological or molecular surveillance, outbreaks, biosafety, or public health implications. Eligible evidence included observational studies such as cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies, as well as outbreak investigations, seroepidemiological studies, ecological and molecular surveillance studies, and other relevant primary investigations. Selected authoritative technical and public health documents were considered when they provided information directly relevant to laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, biosafety, or preparedness. Studies were excluded when they were unrelated to the objectives of the review, provided insufficient information for meaningful interpretation, represented duplicate publications, consisted primarily of opinion or editorial material, or could not provide adequate information for eligibility assessment. Duplicate records identified during the search and screening process were retained only once. 2.4 Study Selection and Screening All records retrieved from the literature search were compiled and screened systematically. The initial search identified 304 records. Duplicate records were removed before screening, after which titles and abstracts were evaluated against the predetermined eligibility criteria. Potentially relevant publications were subsequently assessed through full-text review. Studies that did not satisfy the eligibility criteria at the full-text stage were excluded, with the principal reasons for exclusion documented. Following completion of the screening and eligibility assessment, 18 studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for the final systematic review. The study-selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram showing the progression of records through identification, duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, exclusion, and final inclusion. 2.5 Data Extraction Relevant information was systematically extracted from each included study using a structured data-extraction approach. Extracted variables included, where applicable, the author and year of publication, country or geographical setting, study design, study population or sample, sample size, hantavirus species or strain, diagnostic or laboratory method, exposure or reservoir characteristics, principal findings, and implications for clinical practice, laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, or public health. Particular attention was given to findings relevant to human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, rodent reservoirs, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental risks, and biosafety or laboratory preparedness. The extracted information was organized to permit comparison across the 18 included studies and formed the basis of Table 1, which summarizes the characteristics of the included evidence. 2.6 Methodological Quality and Risk-of-Bias Assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed with consideration of their respective study designs. The appraisal focused on the clarity of the study objectives, appropriateness of study design and participant or specimen selection, adequacy of sample size and methodology, reliability of diagnostic or laboratory procedures, completeness of outcome reporting, and potential sources of selection, measurement, and reporting bias. Quality assessment was used primarily to determine the strength and reliability of the evidence and to guide interpretation of the findings rather than as the sole basis for study exclusion. full_text_sections.full_text: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review Journal Name: Annals of Medical and Health Research: An International Journal DOI: https://doi.org/10.51470/ARMHR.2026.5.1.104 Keywords: Hantavirus, laboratory preparedness, biosafety, molecular diagnosis, serological diagnosis, One Health, surveillance, Philippines Abstract Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness. INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. papers.title: SARS, H1N1, EBOLA, COVID-19, MPOX, H5N1 AND HANTAVIRUS: IS HUMANITY ENTERING A NEW ERA OF PANDEMIC? IS TÜRKİYE PREPARED FOR THE NEXT GLOBAL OUTBREAK?
papers.abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases pose persistent challenges to global health security. Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The emergence and re‑emergence of diseases such as SARS, H1N1, Ebola, COVID‑19, mpox, H5N1 and hantavirus challenge global health security and underscore the need to prepare for unknown “Disease X”. Methods: A descriptive review used a structured literature search and document analysis, with findings organized via a SWOT framework. Results: Strengths include healthcare infrastructure, ICU capacity, digital health and COVID‑19 experience; challenges involve workforce, zoonotic surveillance, public‑health literacy, coordination and external biotech reliance; climate change, travel, migration and trade drive emergence; recommendations focus on integrated surveillance, One‑Health coordination, domestic vaccine/diagnostic capacity and community education, highlighting the need for sustained multisectoral preparedness. papers.title: Epigenetics of HFRS: Linking Immunity, Pathogenesis, and Vaccine-Induced Protection.
papers.abstract: Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV), is an important public-health concern, particularly in Asia. Clinical manifestations range from febrile illness to vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, haemorrhage and acute kidney injury. The mechanisms underlying variation in disease severity and the variability and durability of vaccine-induced immunity remain incompletely understood. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin regulation and non-coding RNA-mediated regulation, can influence antiviral immunity and immune-cell function in several biological settings; however, their specific contributions to HFRS remain insufficiently characterized. This structured narrative review examines hantavirus-specific evidence alongside relevant findings from other viral infections and vaccination settings, focusing on inflammatory responses, endothelial dysfunction, regulatory non-coding RNAs, trained immunity and potential applications in vaccinology. Experimental HTNV studies and clinical investigations of regulatory RNAs have identified candidate pathways associated with hantavirus-host interactions; however, these findings do not establish that epigenetic mechanisms determine HFRS severity or clinical outcomes. Similarly, preclinical hantavirus vaccine studies and early clinical evaluations provide evidence regarding immunogenicity and safety but do not demonstrate epigenetic mediation of protective immunity. Findings from Andes virus (ANDV), associated primarily with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), and other viral systems are therefore considered comparative or contextual evidence, not directly generalizable to HFRS. This review identifies critical knowledge gaps and outlines how longitudinal, cell-resolved epigenomic profiling, functional validation and integrated multi-omics could clarify causal mechanisms, explain interindividual variation in disease outcomes and vaccine responses, and establish the potential translational value of epigenetic biomarkers and interventions.

analysis.background: HFRS, caused by Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus and Seoul virus, is a significant public‑health issue in Asia, with clinical manifestations ranging from fever to vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury; the mechanisms underlying disease severity and vaccine‑induced immunity are incompletely understood.
analysis.methods: The authors conducted a structured narrative review of hantavirus‑specific and comparative viral epigenetic literature, emphasizing inflammatory responses, endothelial dysfunction, regulatory non‑coding RNAs, trained immunity, and vaccinology.
analysis.results: Experimental HTNV studies and clinical investigations have identified candidate epigenetic pathways, but the evidence does not establish that epigenetic mechanisms determine HFRS severity or clinical outcomes; preclinical vaccine studies similarly lack demonstration of epigenetic mediation, and findings from Andes virus and other systems are considered contextual rather than directly generalizable.
analysis.contribution: The review highlights critical knowledge gaps and proposes longitudinal, cell‑resolved epigenomic profiling, functional validation, and integrated multi‑omics to clarify causal mechanisms, explain inter‑individual variation, and explore translational value of epigenetic biomarkers and interventions for HFRS.
analysis.limitations: The work is an abstract‑only narrative review, providing no primary data; conclusions rely on limited, non‑generalizable evidence and the specific contributions of epigenetics to HFRS remain insufficiently characterized.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by Old World hantaviruses (HTNV, SEOV) is a major Asian public‑health concern with a spectrum from fever to severe renal injury, and mechanisms of severity and vaccine immunity are unclear. Methods: A structured narrative review examined hantavirus and comparative viral epigenetic studies focusing on inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, regulatory RNAs, trained immunity, and vaccinology. Results: Candidate epigenetic pathways have been identified, but current evidence does not prove that epigenetic mechanisms drive disease severity or vaccine protection, and findings from other hantaviruses are only contextual. Contribution: The review outlines key knowledge gaps and recommends longitudinal, cell‑resolved epigenomic and multi‑omics approaches to uncover causal mechanisms and potential biomarkers. Limitations: Abstract‑only review with no primary data; evidence is limited and not directly generalizable.

papers.title_zh: 肾综合征出血热的表观遗传学:连接免疫、发病机制与疫苗诱导的保护

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热,由旧世界 汉坦病毒 病毒如 汉滩病毒 和 首尔病毒 引起,是亚洲重要的公共卫生问题,临床表现从发热到血管渗漏、血小板减少、出血和急性肾损伤不等;导致疾病严重程度和疫苗诱导免疫的机制尚未完全阐明。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者对 汉坦病毒 特异性及比较的病毒表观遗传文献进行结构化叙述性综述,重点关注炎症反应、内皮功能障碍、调控性非编码RNA、训练性免疫和疫苗学。
analysis_zh.results: 实验性汉滩病毒研究和临床调查已识别出候选表观遗传通路,但证据尚未证明表观遗传机制决定肾综合征出血热的严重程度或临床结局;临床前疫苗研究同样缺乏表观遗传介导的示例,来自 安第斯病毒 及其他系统的发现被视为情境性而非直接可推广的。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述指出关键知识空白,提出进行纵向、细胞分辨的表观基因组分析、功能验证以及整合多组学,以阐明因果机制,解释个体间差异,并探索表观遗传生物标志物和干预措施在肾综合征出血热中的转化价值。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该工作仅为摘要层面的叙述性综述,未提供原始数据;结论依赖有限、不可推广的证据,表观遗传对肾综合征出血热的具体贡献仍描述不足。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial-coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet-leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

papers.title_zh: 新发和再新发RNA病毒感染中的血管程序:来自SARS-CoV-2、黄病毒和汉坦病毒的比较经验。

analysis_zh.background: 新兴和再现的 RNA 病毒常伴有血管渗漏、血小板功能失调、凝血失衡、微血管损伤和血栓炎症。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该综述将 SARS-CoV-2、黄病毒和 汉坦病毒es 作为病毒诱导血管疾病的互补模型进行比较。
analysis_zh.current_state: 它提出了四个重叠的血管程序——内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板功能障碍——整合了临床、病理和实验证据。
analysis_zh.gaps: 该框架是概念性的,而非定量的,并且缺乏跨病毒的经验验证。
analysis_zh.future_research: 作者建议可检验的预测,包括跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及以表型为导向的临床研究。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：新兴和再现的 RNA 病毒常伴有血管渗漏、血小板功能失调、凝血失衡、微血管损伤和血栓炎症。 主要方向：该综述将 SARS-CoV-2、黄病毒和 汉坦病毒es 作为病毒诱导血管疾病的互补模型进行比较。 研究现状：它提出了四个重叠的血管程序——内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板功能障碍——整合了临床、病理和实验证据。 不足：该框架是概念性的,而非定量的,并且缺乏跨病毒的经验验证。 后续研究：作者建议可检验的预测,包括跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及以表型为导向的临床研究。

papers.title: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic?
papers.abstract: Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT 50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT 50 and PsVNA 50 , respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome and case‑fatality rates up to 50%, motivating vaccine development.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers inactivated vaccines already used in China/Korea and multiple DNA‑vaccine candidates, stratified by platform, target virus, and immunogenicity assay.
analysis.current_state: Ten trials (961 adults) show modest neutralizing seropositivity for inactivated vaccines (45‑56%) and higher binding‑antibody rates, while DNA vaccines achieve up to 100% homologous responses but variable bivalent responses; safety signals are minimal.
analysis.gaps: Safety data remain limited and no validated correlate of protection exists, preventing translation of immunogenicity findings into clinical benefit.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on establishing validated correlates of protection and employing innovative trial designs suited to the low‑incidence nature of hantavirus disease.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause severe hemorrhagic fever with high fatality, prompting vaccine research. Main directions: The review examines inactivated vaccines used in Asia and emerging DNA‑vaccine candidates, organized by platform, virus target, and assay. Current state: Ten trials show modest neutralizing antibody rates for inactivated vaccines and strong homologous responses for DNA vaccines, with minimal serious adverse events. Gaps: Safety remains incompletely characterized and no correlate of protection is validated, limiting clinical interpretation. Future research: Prioritize defining protective correlates and designing trials adapted to the disease's low incidence.

papers.title_zh: 针对汉坦病毒感染的疫苗:系统文献综述。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,致死率最高可达50%,推动疫苗研发。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述涵盖已在中国/韩国使用的灭活疫苗以及多种DNA疫苗候选产品,按平台、靶病毒和免疫原性检测进行分层。
analysis_zh.current_state: 十项临床试验(961名成人)显示灭活疫苗的中和抗体阳性率适中(45‐56%),结合抗体率更高;DNA疫苗可实现最高100%的同源应答,但双价应答呈变异;安全信号极少。
analysis_zh.gaps: 安全性数据仍然有限,且缺乏经验证的保护相关指标,阻碍免疫原性结果向临床获益的转化。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应聚焦于建立经验证的保护相关指标,并采用适合汉坦病毒疾病低发特性的创新试验设计。

papers.title: Host-Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health.
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus , andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host-virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 感染中的宿主-病毒免疫相互作用:对人际传播、发病机制及公共卫生的意义。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)是唯一已知能够在人际间传播并导致严重血管损伤的 汉坦病毒。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述综合了宿主‐病毒免疫相互作用的证据,阐明其在疾病进展、传播动力学以及公共卫生影响中的作用。
analysis_zh.current_state: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)主要攻击肺部内皮细胞,导致血管屏障功能障碍,但并未引起广泛的细胞死亡。
analysis_zh.gaps: 在血液和分泌物中检测到病毒RNA并不等同于确认存在传染性病毒,因而对传染期仍存不确定性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要开展前瞻性研究,结合基因组测序、连续病毒学采样以及标准化的暴露评估,以明确传染阶段和传播模式。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：安第斯病毒(ANDV)是唯一已知能够在人际间传播并导致严重血管损伤的 汉坦病毒。 主要方向：本综述综合了宿主‐病毒免疫相互作用的证据,阐明其在疾病进展、传播动力学以及公共卫生影响中的作用。 研究现状：安第斯病毒(ANDV)主要攻击肺部内皮细胞,导致血管屏障功能障碍,但并未引起广泛的细胞死亡。 不足：在血液和分泌物中检测到病毒RNA并不等同于确认存在传染性病毒,因而对传染期仍存不确定性。 后续研究：需要开展前瞻性研究,结合基因组测序、连续病毒学采样以及标准化的暴露评估,以明确传染阶段和传播模式。
